summary: Belshazzar holds a great feast, drinks from vessels taken from the Jerusalem temple, and praises gods made of metals, wood, and stone. A hand writes on the palace wall, the Babylonian wise men cannot interpret it, and Daniel is summoned to read the writing. Daniel recalls Nebuchadnezzar’s humbling, charges Belshazzar with pride, interprets the words as judgment on the kingdom, and the chapter ends with Belshazzar slain and Darius the Mede receiving the kingdom.
whyItMatters: This chapter is the last court tale set in Babylon before the book moves toward Persian rule and then visions. It shows Daniel’s recurring theme that imperial power can look secure while God’s judgment sets its limit.

context.author: The book does not name a final editor. Traditional readers identify Daniel as author; many critical scholars see a second-century BC final form using older Daniel traditions.
context.audience: Jews pressured to surrender worship, practice, identity, or hope under imperial power.
context.date: The stories are set from the sixth-century BC Babylonian exile into Persian rule. Many scholars date the book’s final Hebrew-Aramaic form to about 167–164 BC, while traditional readings place its origin with Daniel in the sixth century BC.
context.setting: This chapter is set in a Babylonian royal banquet house and palace, with Jerusalem temple vessels brought into the feast.
context.literaryForm: Court tale within Daniel’s Aramaic section, centered on a royal crisis, failed court experts, Daniel’s interpretation, and a sudden reversal of power.

outline.heading: The feast misuses temple vessels
outline.note: Belshazzar gives a large feast, drinks wine from vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem, and praises gods made of various materials.

outline.heading: Writing appears on the wall
outline.note: A hand writes near the lamp stand; the king is terrified, calls the wise men, and learns they cannot read or interpret the writing.

outline.heading: The queen names Daniel
outline.note: The queen enters the banquet house and recalls Daniel as someone known for wisdom, interpretation, and resolving difficult matters.

outline.heading: Daniel is summoned and refuses reward
outline.note: Belshazzar repeats the offer of royal honor, but Daniel says the gifts may go elsewhere while he still agrees to read and interpret the writing.

outline.heading: Daniel recalls Nebuchadnezzar and rebukes Belshazzar
outline.note: Daniel says the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar power, humbled him for pride, and that Belshazzar has not humbled himself despite knowing this.

outline.heading: The writing is interpreted
outline.note: Daniel reads MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN, interprets the kingdom as counted, weighed, and divided, and is then honored as promised.

outline.heading: The kingdom changes hands
outline.note: That night Belshazzar is slain, and Darius the Mede receives the kingdom.

keyVerses.text: In the same hour, the fingers of a man’s hand came out and wrote near the lamp stand on the plaster of the wall of the king’s palace. The king saw the part of the hand that wrote.
keyVerses.why: This is the crisis that interrupts the feast and drives the rest of the chapter.

keyVerses.text: Then Daniel answered before the king, “Let your gifts be to yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king, and make known to him the interpretation.
keyVerses.why: Daniel distances his interpretation from the king’s reward while still agreeing to speak.

keyVerses.text: but have lifted up yourself against the Lord of heaven; and they have brought the vessels of his house before you, and you and your lords, your wives, and your concubines, have drunk wine from them. You have praised the gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which don’t see, or hear, or know; and you have not glorified the God in whose hand your breath is, and whose are all your ways.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers Daniel’s charge against Belshazzar: pride, misuse of the temple vessels, praise of powerless gods, and failure to honor God.

keyVerses.text: TEKEL: you are weighed in the balances, and are found wanting.
keyVerses.why: This is the briefest statement of the chapter’s judgment imagery.

themes: A kingdom counted, weighed, and divided

questions.question: Who is Belshazzar in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter presents Belshazzar as the king hosting the feast and the one judged by the writing on the wall. Historical identification is debated because Belshazzar was historically a crown prince acting for Nabonidus, while the chapter calls him king. The difference between the narrative title and his historical position remains a subject of discussion.

questions.question: Why do the vessels from Jerusalem matter?
questions.answer: The chapter says Nebuchadnezzar had taken golden and silver vessels from the temple in Jerusalem, and Belshazzar has them brought into the feast for drinking. Daniel later treats this as part of Belshazzar lifting himself up against the Lord of heaven. The text does not call the vessels magical; their importance is tied to God’s house and to the king’s public act with them.

questions.question: What are the gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone?
questions.answer: In the feast scene, the guests praise these gods while drinking from the temple vessels. Daniel later says these gods “don’t see, or hear, or know,” contrasting them with “the God in whose hand your breath is.” The chapter’s contrast is between honored objects or deities made from materials and the God who holds life and ways.

questions.question: What are the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers?
questions.answer: They are the court experts Belshazzar calls when the writing appears. The chapter groups them with “the wise men of Babylon,” but says they could not read the writing or make known its interpretation. The point in the chapter is not a detailed taxonomy of their roles, but their inability compared with Daniel’s eventual interpretation.

questions.question: Why does Daniel refuse the king’s gifts if he later receives them?
questions.answer: Daniel tells the king, “Let your gifts be to yourself,” before reading the writing. That refusal shows he is not selling a favorable interpretation or depending on the promised reward. Verse 29 says Belshazzar still orders Daniel clothed with purple and honored, but the honor does not change the judgment Daniel has announced.

questions.question: Why does Daniel talk so much about Nebuchadnezzar?
questions.answer: Daniel uses Nebuchadnezzar as a remembered warning. He says the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar greatness, but when his heart was lifted up he was deposed and humbled until he knew that God rules in human kingdoms. Daniel’s charge is that Belshazzar knew this and still did not humble his heart.

questions.question: What does “father” mean when Nebuchadnezzar is called Belshazzar’s father?
questions.answer: The chapter repeatedly uses “father” for Nebuchadnezzar in relation to Belshazzar. Readers differ on whether to take this as direct ancestry, dynasty language, or a broader royal predecessor relationship. The kings and sequences do not align easily with external chronology, so the safest statement is that the chapter presents Belshazzar in continuity with Nebuchadnezzar and expects him to have learned from him.

questions.question: What do MENE, TEKEL, and PERES mean in the story?
questions.answer: Daniel reads the inscription as “MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN.” He then interprets MENE as God counting the kingdom and ending it, TEKEL as being weighed and found wanting, and PERES as the kingdom divided and given to the Medes and Persians. The terms involve wordplay, and the chapter gives their interpretation through Daniel’s speech.

questions.question: Who is Darius the Mede?
questions.answer: The chapter ends by saying Darius the Mede received the kingdom at about sixty-two years old. The historical identification of Darius the Mede remains difficult and that traditional and critical readers explain this differently. No identification is universally accepted.

glossary.def: Objects from the Jerusalem temple that Belshazzar brings into the feast for drinking; the chapter treats their use as part of his offense.
The place where the feast is happening when the queen enters and speaks to the troubled king.
The explanation of the writing on the wall, which the Babylonian wise men cannot give but Daniel provides.
The weighing image in Daniel’s interpretation of TEKEL, where Belshazzar is judged and found wanting.
